                                                                                                                                                       C1# FM 101-10-1

                                                                                        FOREWORD

                  FM 101—10—1 provides planning data for staff officers at all echelons; however, the primary
              thrust in developing planning data has been to fulfill the needs of planners at division level. Data
              pertaining to TOE’s are#limited to divisional, separate brigade, and armored cavalry regiment.
              FM 101—10—2 contains data pertaining to nondivisional TOE’s.

                  There is a change in format and content in this edition of FM 101—10—1. Revision efforts have
              been directed toward removing unnecessary detail and information readily available in other
              manuals, updating organizational data, and obtaining up-to-date and currently required planning
              factors. Several changes to the manual are incorporated in change 1. Changes in Chapter 2 include
              the addition of combat intelligence companies and new TOE’s for the adjutant general and finance
              companies in all divisions; the addition of division materiel management centers in the AIM
              divisions; new TOE’s for the combat aviation battalion of the infantry division; the replacement of
              the attack helicopter company by an attack helicopter battalion and the replacement of the
              ordnance missile support detachment by a missile support company in the air assault division ; the
              consolidation of the headquarters and main support company of the maintenance battalion and the
              addition of three antiafmor companies in the airborne division; and the addition of a target
              acquisition battery in the AIM and airborne division (cut off date for organizational data is
              November 1976). An operational force requirement planning section has also been added to chapter
              2, and patient admission rates by combat theater have been added to chapter 5. The new chapter 7
              contains situationally dependent combat planning factors including vehicle and tank loss rates,
              ammunition expenditure rates and transportation planning factors.

                  The previous edition of FM 101—10—1 has been criticized for the historical nature of the data it
              presents; i.e., much of the data are based on World War II and the Korean war experience. Where
              possible, data applicable to current organizations and equipment, drawn from these experiences,
              have been validated through comparison with more recent experiences and computer gaming/
              simulation. The historical data, when used for its intended purpose, must be tempered by judgment
              and experience, to be considered valid.

                  During the FM 101—10—1 revision effort, it was discovered that confusion exists in the meaning
              of a “day of supply,” where it is defined, and where and how it is to be used. The planner should
              keep in mind that the average “day of supply” for any class, subclass, or item of supply can vary a
              great deal depending on for example, the size and makeup of the force being planned for, and its
              location. For a large force (in excess of 150,000 men) the proper source, for planning purposes, for
              class V (ammunition) requirements might be Supply Bulletin 38-26, Theater Ammunition Rates, for
              a divisional force the source could be a number of rounds per weapon per day drawn from table
              7—3 (Ammunition per type unit per weapon per day expressed in rounds and STONS). The
              planner should also recognize that regardless of the data source it must be tempered by experience
             and judgment.

                  Commanders and planners must recognize that materiel availability in war is limited.
             Commanders and planners must calculate requirements based on assumptions of disciplined control
             of expenditures and enforced standards of conservation in the execution phase. Austerity requires
             skill, judgment, controls, and command supervision to guard against unnecessary expenditures and
             the accumulation of nonessential stocks. These concepts are significant, difficult to articulate, and
             hard to get into practice, but, austerity and success in battle Eire mutually supporting. Materiel saved
             becomes available for use when really needed. Skilled and disciplined planning and execution are
             essential to mission accomplishment.

                                                                                                     Classes of Supply Legend

CLASS /—Subsistence including gratuitous health and welfare items.
CLASS //—Clothing, individual equipment, tentage, tool sets and tool kits, handtools, administrative and housekeeping supplies and

       equipment. Includes items of equipment, other than principal items prescribed in authonzation/allowance tables and items of
        supply (not including repair parts.)
CLASS III—POL. Petroleum fuels, lubricants, hydraulic and insulating oils, preservatives, liquid and compressed gases, chemical
        products, coolants, deicing and antifreeze compounds, together with components and additives of such products and coal.
CLASS /(^—Construction: Construction materials to include installed equipment and all fortification/barner materials.
CLASS (/—Ammunition. Ammunition of all types (including special ammunition; i.e., chemical and nuclear), bombs, explosives, and
        mines, fuzes, detonators, pyrotechnics, missiles, rockets, propellants, and other associated items.
CLASS (// — Personal Demand Items (nonmilitary sales items).
CLASS (///—Major End Items: A final combination of end products which is ready for its intended use; (principal item), e.g.,
       launchers, tanks, mobile machine shops, vehicles.
CLASS I////—Medical material including medical peculiar repair parts.
CLASS /X—Repair parts and components to include kits, assemblies and subassemblies, reparable and nonreparable required for
        maintenance support of all equipment.
CLASS X—Materiel to support nonmilitary programs; e.g., Agriculture and Economic Development not included in classes I through
        IX.

                                                                                           Subclassifications of Supply L egend

A—Air (aviation, aircraft, airdrop equipment):
        (Class I—Food packet, inflight, individual.)
        (Class 11 —Items of supply and equipment in support of aviation/aircraft.)
        (Class 111—Petroleum and chemical products used in support of aircraft.)
        (Class V—Munitions delivered by aircraft or aircraft weapon systems.)
        (Class VII—Major end items of aviation equipment.)
        (Class IX—Aircraft repair parts.)

B—Troop Support Materiel:
        (Consists of such items as water purification sets, shower, bath, laundry, drycleaning and bakery equipment; sets, kits, and outfits
        (includes tool and equipment sets and shop/equipment sets for performing organization, direct support, general support and
       depot level maintenance operations); sensors and interior intrusion devices; topographic equipment/ and related topographic
       products as outlined in AR 115—11.)

C—Operational Rations:
        (Includes the standard B ration which is used for mass feeding in areas where kitchen facilities, with the exception of refrigeration,
       are available and ration supplement sundries packs issued in conjunction with the standard B ration until normal PX facilities are
       provided.)

D—Commercial Vehicles:
        (Includes wheeled vehicles authorized for use in administrative or tactical operations.)

E—General Supply Items:
        (Includes administrative expendable supplies such as typewriter ribbons, paper, cleaning materials and other supplies normally
       referred to as office supplies. Also includes publications distributed through AG channels.)

F—Clothing and Textiles:
       (Includes individual and organization items of clothing and equipment authorized in allowance tables and teritage/paulins
       authorized in TOE or other media.)

                                     Table 3—2. Ten Classes of Supply—Continued

G—Communications/Electronics (C—E):

(Includes signal items such as radio, telephone, teletype, satellite, avionics, marine communications and navigational equipment;

tactical and nontactical ADP; radar; photographic, audio visual and television equipment; electronic sensors, etc.)

H—Test, Measurement and Diagnostic Equipment (TMDE).

(Includes items of equipment used to determine the operating efficiency or diagnose incipient problems in systems, components,

assemblies and subassemblies of Army used materiel.)

K—Tactical Vehicles:

(Includes trucks, truck tractors, trailers, semitrailers, personnel carriers, etc.)

L—Missiles:

(Classes II, VII and IX include guided missile and rocket systems such as Nike-Hercules, Hawk, Lance, Tow, and Dragon.)

(Class V includes guided missile ammunition items )

M—Weapons.

(Includes small arms, artillery, fire control systems, rocket launchers, machmeguns, air defense weapons, aircraft weapon

subsystems, etc.)

N—Special Weapons:

(Class V—Includes nuclear and thermonuclear munitions.)

(Class VII—Includes weapon systems which deliver nuclear munitions.)

(Class IX—Includes repair parts for class VII—N.)

0—Combat Vehicles.

(Includes main battle tanks, recovery vehicles, self-propelled artillery, armored cars, tracked and half tracked vehicles, etc.)

P—Army Security Agency Materiel:                                                                                         . ,

(Includes that materiel for which CG, US Army Security Agency, has responsibility. Normally authorized in classified

authorization tables. Although ASA items are electronic they are identified separately because they do not follow the same

supply and maintenance channels as subclass G.)

Q—Marine Equipment:
       (Includes marine items of supply and equipment such as amphibious vehicles, landing craft, barges, tugs, floating cranes, dredges,
      etc.)

R—Refrigerated Subsistence.
       (Consist of two categories of refrigeration—that which is required to be maintained at 0 F to keep frozen meals and foods for
      extended periods and that which is to be maintained at approximately 40 F to keep perishables, such as fruits, vegetables, and
      eggs, contained in A rations for shorter periods.)

S—Nonrefrigerated Subsistence'
       (Includes items in standard B rations and nonperishable items in A rations.)

T—Industrial Supplies
       (Common supplies and repair parts such as shop stocks, hardware, and fabrication-type items generally having multiple usage
      and/or application. Such items are generally managed by DISC.)

U—COMSEC Material'
       (This subclass is identified separately from subclass G because of specialized supply and maintenance functions performed
       through a dedicated COMSEC logistic system.)

W—Ground:
       (Class I—Water—when delivered as a supply item.)
       (Class III—Includes petroleum/chemical products and solid fuels used in support of ground and marine equipment.)
       (Class V—Conventional munitions—consists of chemical, smoke, illuminating, incendiary, riot control and improved conventional
       munitions.)
       (Classes 11, VII and I X—Consist of construct ion/road building and materials handling equipment etc.)

X—In Class—indicates no subclass assigned.
V—Railway Equipment:

       (Includes rail items of supply and equipment such as locomotives, railcars, rails, rail joining and shifting equipment, etc.)
Z—Chemical '

       (Classes II, VII and IX—include chemical items such as gas masks, decontaminators, and smoke generators.)
       (Class V—Consists of chemical munitions.)

       pipeline, rail tank car, tank, truck, barge, coastal or ocean-going tankers and stored in a tank or container having a fill capacity
       greater than 500 gallons), 2-Air, Packaged Bulk Fuels (includes fuels in subclass 1 which, because of operational necessity are

generally packaged and supplied in containers of 5- to 55-gallon capacity, except fuels in military collapsible containers of 500
gallons or less which also will be considered as packaged fuels), 3—Air, Packaged Petroleum Products (includes aircraft unique
petroleum and chemical products consisting generally of lubricating oils, greases and specialty items normally packaged by the

Bulk Fuels (includes MOGAS, diesel, kerosene and heating oils, normally transported by pipeline, rail tank car, tank truck, barge,
coastal or ocean going tankers and stored in a tank or container having a fill capacity greater than 500 gallons), 5—Ground,
Packaged Bulk Fuels (includes ground bulk fuels which, because of operational necessity, are generally packaged and supplied in
containers of 5- to 55-gallon capacity, except fuels in military collapsible containers of 500 gallons or less which also will be

4.      The Ration Supplement Sundries Pack is the "frontline post exchange” for use with the B ration before

provided. It consists of a tobacco pack, a toilet article pack, and a confection and stationery pack to meet the requirements of 100

men for one day. It is normally not issued with packaged operational rations, meals, or food packets since these generally contain an

accessory pack which provides all accessory and comfort items critical to their use.

      This is the basic field ration. It consists of such perishables as fresh and frozen meats, vegetables, and fruit. It is intended for use
primarily under stable conditions and during static phases of military operations when normal cooking and refrigeration facilities are
available.

     2
      Same as the field ration, with nonperishables substituted for perishables. It is designed to be used where refrigeration facilities

are lacking or are impracticable but where kitchen and cooking facilities are available (See SB 10—495).
     3
      Designed for use as individual meals or in multiples of 3 for a complete ration. This meal is not to be used over extended periods.
    4
      Issued to troops under special combat conditions where resupply may be uncertain. The principal menu component is

dehydrated and may be eaten as is with drinking water or may be rehydrated rapidly with hot or cold water. Eight different menus
are available.

    5
      Contains four food bars, sugar, instant coffee, and soup and gravy base packed in a rectangular can with a key opener taped to it.

Minimal recommended issue is one-half packet per man per day in hot climates and 1 packet per man per day in cold climates.

       o

      Composed of items necessary to the health and comfort of troops; e.g., essentail toilet articles, tobacco, and confections that
usually are obtained at an exchange. This packet is made available in TO's for issue, pending establishment of adequate service
facilities.

                                                                                                                                            FM 101-10-1

                                                                       FOREWORD

    FM 101—10—1 provides planning data for staff officers at all echelons; however, the primary
thrust in developing planning data has been to fulfill the needs of planners at division level. Data
pertaining to TOE’s are limited to divisional, separate brigade, and armored cavalry regiment.
FM 101—10—2 contains data pertaining to nondivisional TOE’s.

    There is a change in format and content in this edition of FM 101—10—1. Revision efforts have
been directed toward removing unnecessary detail and information readily available in other
manuals, updating organizational structure, and obtaining up-to-date and currently required planning
factors. Although situationally dependent planning factors are provided for ammunition (tables
3—27 through 3—30), for PW capture rates, and for personnel loss rates, work is in progress through
gaming/simulation techniques to expand the data base. When available, this data will be published as
Chapter 7 as part of a Change 1 to the manual.

    The previous edition of FM 101—10—1 has been criticized for the historical nature of the data it
presents; i.e., much of the data are based on World War II and the Korean war experience. Where
possible, data applicable to current organizations and equipment, drawn from these experiences,
have been validated through comparison with more recent experiences. The historical data, when
used for its intended purpose, must be tempered by judgment and experience, to be considered
valid.

    During the FM 101—10—1 revision effort, it was discovered that confusion exists in the meaning
of a “day of supply,” where it is defined, and where and how it is to be used. The planner should
keep in mind that the average “day of supply” for any class, subclass, or item of supply can vary a
great deal depending on for example, the size and makeup of the force being planned for, and its
location. For a large force (in excess of 150,000 men) the proper source, for planning purposes, for
class V (ammunition) requirements might be Supply Bulletin 38-26, Theater Ammunition Rates, for
a divisional force the source could be a number of rounds per weapon per day drawn from table
3—27 (Ammunition per type unit per weapon per day expressed in rounds and STONS). The
planner should also recognize that regardless of the data source it must be tempered by experience
and judgment.

    Commanders and planners must recognize that materiel availability in war is limited.
Commanders and planners must calculate requirements based on assumptions of disciplined control
of expenditures and enforced standards of conservation in the execution phase. Austerity requires
skill, judgment, controls, and command supervision to guard against unnecessary expenditures and
the accumulation of nonessential stocks. These concepts are significant, difficult to articulate, and
hard to get into practice, but, austerity and success in battle are mutually supporting. Materiel saved
becomes available for use when really needed. Skilled and disciplined planning and execution are
essential to mission accomplishment.

     ^This is the basic field ration. It consists of such perishables as fresh and frozen meats, vegetables, and fruit. It is intended for use
